title: Which Way Does an Air Filter Go in an HVAC System?
h1: Which Way Does the Air Filter Go in Your HVAC System?
description: The arrow on an HVAC filter points toward the furnace or air handler, in the direction air flows. Here is how to get it right in every setup.
quick_answer: The arrow on the filter frame should point in the direction the air moves: toward the furnace or air handler and away from the room. At a ceiling return grille, the arrow points up. At a wall grille, it points into the wall. At the furnace, it points toward the blower.
body:
Air filters are built to catch dust from one side. The arrow printed on the frame shows which way the air should flow through it. Put it in backward and the filter still works a little, but it loads up faster, can restrict airflow more and may even let the media pull loose from its frame.

The rule never changes: the arrow follows the air. Air comes out of your rooms, passes through the filter and heads to the blower. So the arrow points away from the room and toward the equipment.

How do I find the airflow direction?

If you're not sure which way the air is moving, here are three easy ways to tell:

  1. Follow the duct. The filter sits between the return grille and the furnace or air handler. Air always moves from the grille toward the equipment.
  2. Use a tissue. With the system running and the grille open, hold a tissue near the filter opening. It will be pulled in the direction of airflow.
  3. Look at the old filter. The side facing the room will be the dirty side. The arrow should point away from it.

Which way does the arrow point in common setups?

Filter locationArrow points
Ceiling return grille, common in hallwaysUp, into the ceiling
Wall return grilleInto the wall, away from you
Upflow furnace in a closet or garage, filter at the bottomUp, toward the blower
Horizontal furnace in the attic, filter at the unitSideways, toward the furnace
Downflow furnace, filter on topDown, toward the blower

In many Southern California homes, the furnace is in the attic and the filter is at a ceiling grille in the hallway. That's the setup where people most often get it backward, because you're installing the filter over your head. The arrow should point up, toward the attic.

What happens if the filter is in backward?

Pleated filters often have a wire backing or a stiffer side meant to face the blower. When the filter is reversed:

  • The media can bow or pull away from the frame under suction
  • Dust may pass around the edges instead of being trapped
  • The filter can clog faster and restrict airflow
  • In bad cases, pieces of the filter can get pulled into the system

One backward filter for a month won't ruin your system. Just flip it the right way or replace it, and check the next one before it goes in.

Does the filter need to fit tightly?

Yes. Direction matters, but fit matters just as much. If the filter is undersized, air slips around the edges and carries dust straight to the blower, coil and ducts. That dust doesn't get caught anywhere until it lands in your rooms.

Use the exact size printed on the old filter. If a grille has noticeable gaps around the filter, a technician can fix the filter rack or seal the opening so all the air goes through the media.

How do I change the filter step by step?

  1. Turn the system off at the thermostat.
  2. Open the grille or filter door and slide out the old filter.
  3. Note the size and the arrow direction on the old one.
  4. Vacuum any dust around the grille or filter slot.
  5. Slide in the new filter with the arrow pointing toward the equipment.
  6. Close the grille or door fully and turn the system back on.

Writing the date on the filter frame with a marker makes it easy to know when it's due next.

How often should I change it?

Check a 1-inch filter monthly and plan on replacing it every one to three months. Homes with pets, ongoing projects or heavy fan use need more frequent changes. After a Santa Ana wind event or a stretch of wildfire smoke, check it right away, since it can load up fast.

If your filters keep clogging quickly or the grille whistles, the system may have an airflow or duct leak problem. Our indoor air quality team can check your filter setup and suggest a better option if one fits your system.
faqs: Which side of the air filter faces the furnace?
The side the arrow points toward faces the furnace or air handler. The opposite side faces the room or the return grille, and that's the side that gets dirty.
What if my filter has no arrow?

Some filters are the same on both sides and can go either way. If the filter has a wire mesh or stiffer backing on one side, that side goes toward the blower. When in doubt, buy filters that have an arrow.
Can a backward filter damage my system?

Usually not right away, but it can let dust bypass the filter, clog faster and restrict airflow. Over time, low airflow can freeze the AC coil or overheat the furnace. Flip it or replace it as soon as you notice.
Why does my filter get sucked into the grille?

That usually means the filter is too restrictive, too clogged or doesn't fit the frame. It can also mean the return is undersized for the system. Try a correctly sized filter, and if it still bends, have the airflow checked.
